content: Cefixime is a third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic that has been approved by the FDA for the treatment of several bacterial infections, including uncomplicated urinary tract infections, otitis media, pharyngitis, tonsillitis, acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, and uncomplicated gonorrhea. The most common side effects associated with cefixime include diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, dyspepsia, and vomiting. For adults, the recommended dosage of cefixime is 400 mg daily. This can be administered as a single 400 mg tablet or capsule once daily, or as a divided dose of 200 mg every 12 hours. For specific infections: Uncomplicated urinary tract infections caused by Escherichia coli and Proteus mirabilis can be treated with the standard dosage. Otitis media caused by Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and Streptococcus pyogenes is treated with cefixime. Pharyngitis and tonsillitis caused by Streptococcus pyogenes require a therapeutic dosage for at least 10 days. Acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae are treated with cefixime. Uncomplicated gonorrhea (cervical or urethral) caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae is treated with a single oral dose of 400 mg. For pediatric patients aged six months or older, the recommended dose is 8 mg/kg/day, which can be given as a single daily dose or divided into two doses of 4 mg/kg every 12 hours. Children weighing more than 45 kg or older than 12 years should receive the adult dosage. Cefixime chewable tablets must be chewed or crushed before swallowing. The same infections treated in adults can also be treated in pediatric patients, with appropriate dosage adjustments. Cefixime is contraindicated in patients with known allergies to cefixime or other cephalosporins. Hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported. Patients with a history of penicillin allergy should be treated with caution due to the potential for cross-reactivity. If an allergic reaction occurs, the drug should be discontinued immediately. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with cefixime use and can range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. CDAD should be considered in any patient presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use, even if symptoms occur up to two months after treatment. If CDAD is suspected, discontinuation of the antibiotic and appropriate management, including fluid and electrolyte replacement, protein supplementation, and specific treatment for C. difficile, should be initiated. In patients with renal impairment, the dosage of cefixime should be adjusted. Those undergoing continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) or hemodialysis (HD) should be monitored carefully, as cefixime is not significantly removed by dialysis. Cephalosporins, including cefixime, may cause a reduction in prothrombin activity, particularly in patients with renal or hepatic impairment, poor nutritional status, or those on prolonged antimicrobial therapy. Monitoring of prothrombin time and administration of vitamin K may be necessary in at-risk patients. Cefixime should only be prescribed for confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial infections to avoid the development of drug-resistant bacteria. Prescribing cefixime in the absence of a bacterial infection is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of resistance. Adverse reactions observed in clinical trials include gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhea (16%), loose stools (6%), abdominal pain (3%), nausea (7%), dyspepsia (3%), and flatulence (4%). Rare but serious adverse reactions include pseudomembranous colitis, anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis. Laboratory abnormalities such as elevated liver enzymes, hyperbilirubinemia, and changes in blood cell counts have also been reported. Cefixime may interact with other drugs. For example, co-administration with carbamazepine may increase carbamazepine levels, and concurrent use with warfarin or other anticoagulants may prolong prothrombin time, increasing the risk of bleeding. Cefixime may also cause false-positive results in certain urine glucose tests and the Coombs test. In pregnancy, cefixime is classified as Category B by the FDA, indicating that animal studies have not shown harm to the fetus, but adequate studies in pregnant women are lacking. It should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. It is unknown whether cefixime is excreted in human milk, so nursing mothers should consider discontinuing breastfeeding during treatment. Cefixime is primarily excreted unchanged in the urine, with a serum half-life of 3 to 4 hours in healthy individuals. In patients with renal impairment, the half-life may be prolonged, necessitating dosage adjustments. The drug is not significantly removed by hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis. Patients should be counseled to complete the full course of therapy as prescribed, even if symptoms improve early, to prevent treatment failure and the development of antibiotic resistance. They should also be advised to report any severe or persistent diarrhea, as this may indicate C. difficile infection. Cefixime is available in various formulations, including tablets, capsules, chewable tablets, and oral suspension. It should be stored at 20 to 25°C (68 to 77°F).
